body.statement: The interval \(I_{T,\Delta}\) is \(O_{T,\Delta}\)-measurable and uniformly honest over \(\mathfrak M_T(\alpha,\beta,L,c,C,\varepsilon)\cup\mathfrak M_T^{\mathrm{low}}(\alpha,\beta,L,c,\varepsilon)\), without conditioning on \(E_T\) and without convergence of \(t^\alpha\pi_t(1)\). Measurability follows from the recorded calendar revelation times, including when a response remains unrevealed at \(H_T\). On \(\mathfrak M_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{reg}}(\kappa)\), assign the displayed studentized quotient the value zero on \(E_T^c\). Then \(\sup_x|P\{(\widehat\tau_{T,\Delta}-\tau+b_{T,\Delta})/\widehat s_{T,\Delta}\leq x\}-\Phi(x)|\to0\) and \(\widehat s_{T,\Delta}/s_{T,\Delta}\to1\) uniformly.
body.justification: This is the load-bearing uniform studentization result that makes one implementable procedure valid in both Gaussian and degenerate regimes.
body.gap: Bibaut et al., Hadad et al., and Shi, Wang, and Wu rely on centered scores plus variance consistency or convergence; none treats an outcome-selected reveal process with an overlapping correction and an observable low-variance splice.
body.consumer: The theorem yields a prespecifiable implementation that does not fail when the inferior-arm outcome variance is small or the adaptive allocation oscillates.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(K_a=K_a(n_T)\), \(J_a=K_a(k_T)\), and
\[
 \sigma_{a,T}^2=\operatorname{Var}_P(X_{a,1}^{\Delta}),
 \qquad
 Z_T=(M_{1,\Delta}-PM_{1,\Delta})-(M_{0,\Delta}-PM_{0,\Delta}),
\]
\[
 C_T=(U_{1,\Delta}-PU_{1,\Delta})-(U_{0,\Delta}-PU_{0,\Delta}).
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem:arm\text{-}tape\text{-}equivalence}\), these are functions of deterministic prefixes of independent, identically distributed arm tapes.  By \(\mathrm{lem:old\text{-}cohort\text{-}correction}\), on \(E_T\),
\[
 \widehat\tau_{T,\Delta}-\tau+b_{T,\Delta}=Z_T+C_T. \tag{1}
\]
This is an unconditional identity in the tape variables; \(E_T\) only determines whether the observable estimator uses those prefixes.

First note that the delay envelope rules out infinite delays.  For each arm, continuity from above and \(\beta>0\) give
\[
 P\{D(a)=\infty\}=\lim_{u\to\infty}P\{D(a)>u\}
 \leq \lim_{u\to\infty}L(1+u)^{-\beta}=0. \tag{2}
\]
We next verify measurability.  On \(E_T\), the first \(K_a\) assignments to arm \(a\) occur no later than \(n_T\), and hence their ages at \(H_T\) are at least
\[
 H_T-n_T=m_T+\Delta_T=g_{T,\Delta}.
\]
The first \(J_a\) assignments occur no later than \(k_T\), and their ages are at least
\[
 H_T-k_T=h_{T,\Delta}.
\]
If one of these responses is revealed, \(O_{T,\Delta}\) records its outcome, delay, and revelation time.  If it is absent at \(H_T\), its delay exceeds the applicable guaranteed age, so its contribution to the corresponding truncated variable is known to be zero.  Thus every \(X_{a,j}^{\Delta}\), \(R_{a,j}^{\Delta}\), sample variance, gate, and endpoint is \(O_{T,\Delta}\)-measurable on \(E_T\).  The definitions on \(E_T^c\) are functions of the observed assignment counts, so the complete interval is measurable.

We establish a finite-sample guarantee for the concentration branch.  If \(X\in[-1,1]\), convexity of the exponential on this interval, followed by centering, gives
\[
 P\exp\{\lambda(X-PX)\}\leq \exp(\lambda^2/2).
\]
Multiplication over the independent tape variables, exponential Markov inequality, and optimization over \(\lambda\) yield
\[
 P\{|Z_T|>\sqrt{2S_Tx}\}\leq 2e^{-x},
 \qquad S_T=K_1^{-1}+K_0^{-1}. \tag{3}
\]
For \(R=Y\mathbf 1\{g_{T,\Delta}<D\leq h_{T,\Delta}\}\), bounded outcomes and the delay envelope imply
\[
 |R-PR|\leq2,
 \qquad P(R-PR)^2\leq PR^2\leq v_{T,\Delta}.
\]
Moreover, for every integer \(j\geq2\),
\[
 P|R-PR|^j\leq2^{j-2}P(R-PR)^2.
\]
Expanding the exponential series and applying exponential Markov inequality therefore gives the Bernstein bound
\[
 P\left\{|U_{a,\Delta}-PU_{a,\Delta}|>
 \sqrt{\frac{2v_{T,\Delta}x}{J_a}}+\frac{4x}{3J_a}\right\}
 \leq2e^{-x}. \tag{4}
\]
The displayed linear term is conservative relative to the value obtained by direct optimization.  Taking \(x=x_\eta=\log(6/\eta)\), the union of the exceptional events in (3) and the two instances of (4) has probability at most \(\eta\).  On its complement, (1), the triangle inequality, and \(|b_{T,\Delta}|\leq B_{T,\Delta}\) imply \(\tau\in I_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{conc}}\) whenever \(E_T\) occurs.  Since \(\tau\in[-2,2]\), intersection with \([-2,2]\) cannot remove the target, and on \(E_T^c\) the reported interval is \([-2,2]\).  Consequently this coverage argument is unconditional and does not condition on quota success.

It remains to validate the Gaussian branch and the observable splice.  Define
\[
 V_T=\sigma_{1,T}^2+\mathbf 1\{\alpha=0\}\sigma_{0,T}^2.
\]
Consider first an arbitrary triangular sequence of laws for which \(V_T\geq1/\log T\).  When \(\alpha>0\),
\[
 s_{T,\Delta}^2\geq\frac{1}{K_1\log T};
\]
when \(\alpha=0\), the quota orders in \(\mathrm{lem:quota\text{-}success}\) give \(s_{T,\Delta}^2\geq c_0/(T\log T)\) for a constant \(c_0>0\).  Express \(Z_T/s_{T,\Delta}=\sum_j\xi_{Tj}\) as the sum of its independent centered tape summands.  Their variances sum to one.  Bounded outcomes and the preceding variance lower bounds give
\[
 \delta_T^*:=\max_j|\xi_{Tj}|
 =O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log T}{K_1}}\right)=o(1)
 \quad(\alpha>0),
\]
and \(\delta_T^*=O(\sqrt{\log T/T})=o(1)\) when \(\alpha=0\).  These bounds are uniform over the stated variance regime because \(K_1\asymp T^{1-\alpha}\).

For fixed real \(u\), Taylor's formula with \(|\xi_{Tj}|\leq\delta_T^*\) gives
\[
 P e^{iu\xi_{Tj}}
 =1-\frac{u^2}{2}P\xi_{Tj}^2
 +O\bigl(|u|^3\delta_T^*P\xi_{Tj}^2\bigr).
\]
Also
\[
 \sum_j(P\xi_{Tj}^2)^2
 \leq (\delta_T^*)^2\sum_jP\xi_{Tj}^2=(\delta_T^*)^2.
\]
Taking logarithms and summing proves
\[
 P\exp\{iuZ_T/s_{T,\Delta}\}=\exp\{-u^2/2+o(1)\}. \tag{5}
\]
The error is uniform.  The unit second moment gives tightness, and (5) identifies every subsequential limit as standard normal.  A contradiction-subsequence argument, using continuity of the Gaussian distribution function, therefore yields
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T):,V_T\geq1/\log T}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
 \left|P\{Z_T/s_{T,\Delta}\leq x\}-\Phi(x)\right|\longrightarrow0. \tag{6}
\]
This derives the Gaussian limit from bounded summands and the deterministic quota orders; no limit of \(t^\alpha\pi_t(1)\) is used.

The correction need not be independent of \(Z_T\).  The variance bound in \(\mathrm{lem:old\text{-}cohort\text{-}correction}\) and the quota orders give
\[
 PC_T^2=O\bigl(T^{-\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)}\bigr).
\]
In both cases \(\alpha>0\) and \(\alpha=0\), the variance lower bound above implies
\[
 \frac{PC_T^2}{s_{T,\Delta}^2}
 \leq C_1(\log T)T^{1-\alpha-\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)}\longrightarrow0, \tag{7}
\]
because \(\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)>1-\alpha\).

For a sample of size \(K\geq2\), the usual sample variance is
\[
 \widehat\sigma^2=\frac{K}{K-1}\{\overline{X^2}-\bar X^2\}.
\]
Since \(|X|\leq1\), Chebyshev's inequality applied to \(\overline{X^2}\) and \(\bar X\) gives, uniformly in the tape law,
\[
 \widehat\sigma_{X,a,\Delta}^2-\sigma_{a,T}^2=O_P(K_a^{-1/2}). \tag{8}
\]
When \(\alpha>0\), division by \(s_{T,\Delta}^2\geq1/(K_1\log T)\) bounds the relative arm-one error by
\[
 O_P(\log T/\sqrt{K_1})=o_P(1),
\]
and the arm-zero error by
\[
 O_P(K_1\log T/K_0^{3/2})=o_P(1).
\]
When \(\alpha=0\), both quotas are comparable to \(T\), and division by \(c_0/(T\log T)\) gives the same conclusion.  Hence
\[
 \widehat s_{T,\Delta}/s_{T,\Delta}\longrightarrow1 \tag{9}
\]
uniformly on \(V_T\geq1/\log T\).  Equations (1), (6), (7), and (9), together with \(P(E_T^c)\leq4T^{-4}\), imply the uniform studentized approximation on this regime.  Assigning the quotient the value zero on \(E_T^c\) changes its distribution function by at most \(P(E_T^c)\).

The regular class eventually lies in this high-variance regime.  Indeed, for \(X=Y\mathbf 1\{D\leq g_{T,\Delta}\}\), boundedness gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\operatorname{Var}(X)-\operatorname{Var}(Y)|
 &\leq |P(X^2-Y^2)|+|(PX)^2-(PY)^2|\\
 &\leq3P\{D>g_{T,\Delta}\}
 \leq3v_{T,\Delta}. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
Since \(g_{T,\Delta}\geq m_T\to\infty\), the right side tends to zero uniformly.  The regular-variance assumption thus gives \(V_T\geq\kappa/2\) eventually, also when \(\alpha=0\) after adding the two bounds in (10).  This proves both studentization assertions over \(\mathfrak M_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm{reg}}(\kappa)\).

We now prove coverage for the Gaussian radius.  Put
\[
 f_B(s)=s c_\eta(B/s),\qquad s>0.
\]
If \(Z\) is standard normal, the defining equation for \(c_\eta\) and monotonicity in the magnitude of the shift imply, for every \(|b|\leq B\),
\[
 P\{|sZ-b|\leq f_B(s)\}
 =\Phi(c_\eta(B/s)+b/s)+\Phi(c_\eta(B/s)-b/s)-1
 \geq1-\eta. \tag{11}
\]
Let \(u=B/s\) and \(x=c_\eta(u)-u\).  The defining equation implies
\[
 z_{1-\eta}\leq x\leq z_{1-\eta/2},
 \qquad
 B+z_{1-\eta}s\leq f_B(s)\leq B+z_{1-\eta/2}s. \tag{12}
\]
Implicit differentiation gives
\[
 c_\eta'(u)=
 \frac{\phi(c_\eta(u)-u)-\phi(c_\eta(u)+u)}
 {\phi(c_\eta(u)-u)+\phi(c_\eta(u)+u)}\in[0,1]
\]
and therefore
\[
 f_B'(s)=x+
 \frac{2u\phi(x+2u)}{\phi(x)+\phi(x+2u)}.
\]
This derivative is bounded uniformly in \(B\geq0\) and \(s>0\): use \(x\geq z_{1-\eta}>0\) and
\[
 \frac{\phi(x+2u)}{\phi(x)}=\exp\{-2ux-2u^2\}.
\]
Thus (9) implies \(f_{B_{T,\Delta}}(\widehat s_{T,\Delta})-f_{B_{T,\Delta}}(s_{T,\Delta})=o_P(s_{T,\Delta})\), uniformly on the high-variance regime.  Combining this Lipschitz bound, (11), and the uniform Kolmogorov approximation already proved shows that
\[
 \inf_{(P,\Pi,T):,V_T\geq1/\log T}
 P\{\tau\in I_{T,\Delta}^{\mathrm G}\}\geq1-\eta-o(1). \tag{13}
\]
For completeness, this last implication follows by shrinking the deterministic interval in (11) by \(\epsilon s_{T,\Delta}\), paying at most \(2\epsilon/\sqrt{2\pi}\) under the Gaussian law, then using (6)--(9), and finally letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\).  The nonnegative term \(d_{T,\Delta}\) can only enlarge the interval.

The quota orders and the two strict inequalities imposed on \(\rho\) give
\[
 d_{T,\Delta}
 =O\left(
 \sqrt{T^{-\rho(\beta+1-\alpha)}\log T}
 +T^{-\rho(1-\alpha)}\log T\right)
 =o(T^{-(1-\alpha)/2}). \tag{14}
\]
It remains to check the data-dependent splice.  If \(V_T\leq1/\log T\), (8) and Chebyshev's inequality imply
\[
 \sup_{(P,\Pi,T):,V_T\leq1/\log T}P(G_{T,\Delta})
 \leq C_2(\log T)^2/K_1\longrightarrow0. \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, gate success requires the relevant sample-variance sum to exceed its population counterpart by at least \(1/\log T\).  Hence in this regime the selected interval equals the concentration interval except on an event of probability \(o(1)\).

If \(V_T>1/\log T\), then on \(G_{T,\Delta}^c\), the deterministic gate inequality and the bound \(\widehat\sigma^2\leq2\) imply
\[
 \widehat s_{T,\Delta}^2
 \leq \frac{2}{K_1\log T}+\frac{2}{K_0}
 =o(T^{-(1-\alpha)})
 \quad(\alpha>0),
\]
whereas \(\widehat s_{T,\Delta}^2=O(1/(T\log T))\) when \(\alpha=0\).  Thus \(\widehat s_{T,\Delta}=o(T^{-(1-\alpha)/2})\) uniformly on gate failure.  Moreover
\[
 a_T=\sqrt{2S_Tx_\eta}\asymp T^{-(1-\alpha)/2}.
\]
By (12) and (14), for all sufficiently large \(T\),
\[
 f_{B_{T,\Delta}}(\widehat s_{T,\Delta})+d_{T,\Delta}
 \leq B_{T,\Delta}+a_T.
\]
The concentration radius is at least \(B_{T,\Delta}+a_T\).  Therefore, on gate failure the concentration interval contains the Gaussian interval; on gate success the selected interval is the Gaussian interval.  By (13), the selected interval is uniformly honest in the high-variance regime.  By (3)--(4) and (15), it is uniformly honest in the low-variance regime.  The full interval on \(E_T^c\) completes the proof over both declared model classes, without conditioning on quota success or assuming convergence of the scaled propensity.
